justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon are driven by the best available data at the time of the forecast, which includes historical trends, any prevailing patterns in recent observations, and the assumption that the underlying drivers of the variable being forecasted are relatively stable over time. In this case, the point estimates across all horizons (one day, one week, and one month) are the same because they reflect the central or "most likely" value based on the current data. Essentially, it's like saying: if nothing significant changes, this is the value we expect to see on average over any time frame.

The uncertainty captured in the confidence intervals (CIs) increases as the forecast horizon gets longer. Over one day, there is minimal opportunity for volatility or unforeseen events to disrupt the trend, which is why the 90% CI—from 283.67 to 287.39—is relatively narrow. Moving to one week, variability from factors like market fluctuations, short-term news, or small shocks in the system starts to compound, so the confidence interval widens (278.94 to 292.12). Over one month, the uncertainty grows even larger, accounting for harder-to-predict changes such as more significant trends or external disruptions, leading to the widest interval (270.25 to 300.81). This reflects the natural progression of uncertainty as forecasts extend further into the future.

There are always specific risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals, as no model or forecast can perfectly predict the future. For example, a sudden geopolitical event, a shift in economic policy, an unexpected technological advancement, or even new data invalidating the current assumptions could cause deviations well beyond the CIs. Additionally, the model assumes normal or expected conditions; disruptions outside normal expectations, such as black swan events, are inherently difficult to factor in and could lead to outcomes beyond the bounds of the forecast.
